Disclaimer Links PAGES on NUCLEAR ISSUES EU considers emergency meeting as nuclear shutdown leaves Hungary facing energy crisis By Sandor Zsiros , 31/07/2026, https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/07/31/eu-considers-emergency-meeting-as-nuclear-shutdown-leaves-hungary-facing-energy-crisis Hungarian PM Péter Magyar has warned of an energy crisis after record-low Danube water levels forced the shutdown of the Paks nuclear plant, which supplies nearly half the country’s power. The European Commission says it is prepared to convene an emergency meeting of its Electricity Coordination Group over the shutdown of Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant, as the country’s prime minister warned of a looming energy crisis. “Although the operator has emergency measures in place to guarantee nuclear safety, an event of this kind could further strain the regional electricity balance,” the Commission’s spokesperson, Anna-Kaisa Itkonen, told Euronews. “The Commission stands ready to convene an ad hoc meeting of the Electricity Coordination Group.” Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has warned that the country could face an energy crisis as early as next week, after Paks – which supplies almost half of Hungary’s energy needs – was taken offline following record-low water levels in the Danube, which is used to cool the reactors. It is the first time the plant has been shut down completely since it opened 42 years ago. “This means 2,000 megawatts will be lost from Hungarian energy production from Monday at the latest, while demand for residential and public consumption continues to rise because of the heat,” Magyar said on Thursday evening. The government has asked the public and businesses to cut energy use during the peak hours between 5pm and 10pm, urging people to avoid using air conditioning and washing machines in particular. Magyar explained that the government has also drawn up an emergency plan to limit consumption at industrial facilities on a rotational basis. The output of other power plants in Hungary will also be increased. “Given the severity of this unprecedented situation, we are asking everyone – large consumers and the public alike – to act responsibly,” he said. “It is in our common interest to avoid unplanned outages and the kind of unexpected system collapse seen in Western Europe and the Balkans.” András Perger, an expert at the Hungarian NGO Energiaklub, told Euronews that the country stands to lose 25–30 percent of its energy output from Monday, describing the situation as a serious test of Hungary’s energy supply. “From Monday, when consumption is expected to rise and the Paks plant remains offline, a more serious situation will begin,” Perger said. “This will be a serious test for Hungarian and regional supply alike.” He added that some of Hungary’s demands could be met through imports from neighbouring countries, though the availability of hydroelectric power is itself limited in the region. In Romania, the shutdown of one reactor poses less of a problem, given that nuclear energy makes up a smaller share of the country’s energy mix. “Although the situation in Hungary is stretched, I don’t expect this to cause serious regional problems,” Perger said. Friends of the Earth Hungary, an environmental NGO says the development around the Paks Nuclear Plant is not an isolated incident but a climate adaptation challenge. “Hungary needs to speed up its transition into a more resilient, decentralised energy system that relies less on climate-vulnerable infrastructure and more on energy savings, flexibility and renewable energy,” Executive President Ákos Éger said in a statement sent to Euronews. The Commission’s Itkonen said Brussels is closely monitoring the electricity supply situation in both Hungary and Romania, though she stressed there are currently no immediate energy security concerns. According to the Commission, the Electricity Coordination Group could aim to facilitate information-sharing and coordinate next steps among countries in the region. The process will be watched closely as Hungary heads into what officials on both sides describe as a critical test of the country’s energy resilience. https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: Welcome to the geek corner. Serbia’s electoral system is both straightforward and complicated, which makes it a nightmare to explain in a short blog post. Generally, we are talking about a 250-seat parliament, and it’s a race to 126 in terms of securing a majority. There is only one constituency, and you vote for a closed party list, not a specific candidate. So far, so good. The electoral threshold is generally 3%, but there are exceptions from this rule for national minority parties and they may or may not be relevant when determining the outcome of the vote. Over to Florian Bieber of the University of Graz: “What is important is not just the support for the two big lists, but it’s also about whether the smaller parties make it into parliament. We’re talking about three parties which are really on the threshold. I expect them not to [get in], but again, we don’t know for sure. There’s the Socialists, which are the long-term coalition partners, and they seem to be in crisis, and Vucic

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Religious Israelis walk past a polling station in Bet Shemesh on Tuesday. Turnout is expected to shatter records. Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Religious Israelis walk past a polling station in Bet Shemesh on Tuesday. Turnout is expected to shatter records. Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty Images Israel Legacy of 7 October looms large as a divided Israel goes to the polls in record numbers Bereaved families tell voters to remember the victims while others have flown thousands of miles to cast their ballots Emma Graham-Harrison in Efrat and Julian Borger in Nazareth Tue 27 Oct 2026 15.47 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 16.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Election day in Israel began with a protest by some of the voters with most at stake. Bereaved families of those killed in the 7 October attacks held a minute of silence at 6.29am, the moment when Hamas launched its onslaught just over three years ago. They gathered in a Tel Aviv plaza that has become known as “hostages square” because it was the centre of demonstrations demanding the return of more than 200 captives from Gaza . Holding pictures of their loved ones, they stood in silence then called on voters to remember the losses and betrayals of that day when deciding on the next government. “Three years after the massacre, our loved ones will not be voting today. Go out and vote – remember them at the ballot box. This is what these elections are about,” the group said. They are not explicitly backing any political party, but one of their key demands is a state commission of inquiry into the attacks. Benjamin Netanyahu has resisted this and it has become a rallying point for the opposition parties trying to unseat him as prime minister. View image in fullscreen Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, casts his vote in Herzliya. He said Benjamin Netanyahu had led the worst government Israel had known. Photograph: Shir Torem/Reuters Netanyahu’s strongest challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, started the day by visiting communities attacked on 7 October. “If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here,” said the former military chief and leader of the Yashar party. Standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of “the worst government Israel has known”. He noted that victory wasn’t certain, adding that “we are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state”. As the day wore on, it became clear that voter turnout was shattering all records and among those lining up at polling stations were tens of thousands of Israelis who live overseas. View image in fullscreen A polling station in the Jewish settlement of Efrat in the West Bank. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian A bipartisan “Fly&Vote” initiative was set up to support those who wanted to return because electoral law only allows voting in person. While not everyone coming back was opposed to the government, anecdotal evidence suggested many were opposition supporters who held the view that Israel faced an existential choice. Monica Moria, 58, and her husband, Ron, flew in to Tel Aviv from Barcelona. They took a train to a kibbutz where she is registered to vote and she cast her ballot for the most leftwing of the Jewish Israeli parties, the Democrats. She said: “It feels like Israel has lost its way, there are deep divisions and hatreds that will be very difficult to heal. The idea is to bring a political change so that we can bring Israeli society together again. I want to be optimistic, but I am also afraid.” Kobi Mizrahi, 35, who has been completing a PhD in New York, paid more than $1,600 (£1,200) to come back to Israel for just a few days and vote. He said: “Given the fact that it feels like a ‘now or never’ moment, where if we lose these elections to the Bibi coalition this might be the turning point we can’t come back to, I felt like I have to do anything in my power to help.” View image in fullscreen Yuval Schwarzfuchs, right, flew all the way from Rio de Janeiro to vote for the Joint List in Jerusalem. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian Yuval Schwarzfuchs, 26, travelled from Rio de Janeiro via Ethiopia to vote for the Palestinian-led Joint List. “For me, its about equality for all,” he said. “I did what I had to do.” He came to the Jerusalem polling station wearing a T-shirt with an image of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the leftwing president of Brazil, who defied the polls to win re-election at the weekend. In the settlement of Efrat near Jerusalem, Shani, 19, had come to the polling station with her parents, to cast her vote for the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich. She is part of a large cohort of first-time voters who are more rightwing than older generations and may help bolster support for Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners. More than 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the last election in 2022, and three-quarters of first-time Jewish voters define themselves as right or centre-right, a poll for Channel 12 television found (it did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel). Shani said she chose Smotrich, a settler himself, for his promises to expand Israel’s footprint in occupied Palestine . “Smotrich is pushing forward with settlement expansion and improving security,” she said. Her mother, kindergarten teacher Rivka, also voted for Smotrich, and said her priority was to return Netanyahu’s coalition to office. View image in fullscreen A Palestinian family walks past election campaign posters in Beit Kahil in the West Bank on Tuesday. Palestinian parties in Israel may hold the balance of power in what is expected to be a tight result. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images “The right must win, because otherwise there is a chance of a Palestinian state, which will be very bad for Jews,” she said. Spiralling attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinians, and the growing threat of sanctions on settlement goods and construction, were not a key election issue for voters in Efrat who spoke to the Guardian. The Palestinian Israeli vote is a critical camp in this election, representing about a fifth of eligible voters. Their votes are expected to go to either Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, or Joint List, an electoral alliance of Palestinian-Israeli parties. Even if the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot wins more seats than Netanyahu’s coalition, it is not expected to win an outright majority. It has also ruled out going into coalition with the Palestinian Israeli parties, which could well hold the balance of power. Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the leading party in the Joint List coalition, thinks Eisenkot’s approach may change after the elections. “He cannot sit down [in coalition] with Netanyahu, and he won’t want to go back to another round of elections, so we think he can be flexible,” he said. View image in fullscreen Arab voters who are Israeli citizens cast their ballots at a polling station in Nazareth, Israel. Turnout was high in the city. Photograph: Adri Salido/Anadolu/Getty Images In Nazareth, the largest Palestinian-majority town in Israel, the turnout at polling stations has been noticeably higher than at recent elections, although still below the average Jewish turnout across the country. A surge of evening voting was expected here as people came home from work. At the headquarters of the Joint List, the most pressing concern was the spoiler tactics of far-right election monitors at predominantly Palestinian polling stations. “They can say that they want to check all the voter numbers and identity and everything, so they can slow things down, so that people wait a long time and give up. That’s their intention,” said Shbita. At worst, these ploys have slowed the process down so that it took half an hour to vote, rather than a couple of minutes, he added. Shbita said voters were sufficiently motivated to overcome such obstacles. “It is the first time for a long time that a government has stayed in office for its full term, four years,” he said. “We are talking about one of the worst governments when it comes to Arab society. We feel racism at all levels of Israeli society, in hospitals, in buses, in public transportation, in the media. So people understand that today we have the opportunity to change the government.” Explore more on these topics Israel Palestine Gaza Benjamin Netanyahu Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.heraldgoa.in/cafe/angela-tri.text: SHARE Vivek Menezes An unknown major work by the sadly neglected Indian modernist Angela Trindade (1909-1980) has abruptly emerged to attention from the unlikely location of the salon of the Consul General of Portugal at Altinho in Panjim. Along with three additional paintings by the same pioneering artist, the magnificent Coronation of Our Lady (1947) was recently borrowed from the Fundação Oriente collection, but this exceptionally large and detailed water colour has never been displayed in public, and is not included in Fatima da Silva Gracias’s authoritative 2016 Angela Trindade: A Trinity of Light, Colour and Emotion. I was riveted at first sight last week, across the room in a reception hosted by Ambassador Manuela Franco, and am most grateful to the dynamic FO director Paulo Gomes for promptly responding to my request to send across the scan printed on this page. - Advertisement - If you enjoyed reading this article, you can help support our journalism by adding OHeraldo as a preferred source. There is so much happening in this amazing formally Indian Christian rendering of the “fifth glorious mystery” where Christ, God the Father and the Holy Spirit (in the form of a dove) are depicted crowning Mary as Queen of Heaven. You can see Trindade took this painting very seriously, giving it everything she had: her full JJ School training with its emphasis on ancient Indian art (especially the Ajanta frescoes); wholehearted nationalist politics, with dark-skinned figures interspersed as equals; and an unquenched feminist spirit, with women and girls outnumbering males in her vision of paradise. When I sent the image to Rupert Arrowsmith, the excellent UK based scholar, he pointed out “pan Asianism in the era of decolonisation, that recalls the original pan-Asianism of Buddhism itself.” To me it is clear that Coronation of Our Lady was a kind of manifesto for Angela Trindade in the exhilarating cusp of Indian independence, a summing-up and perhaps a kind of farewell, because the artist began regular back-and-forth to the USA soon afterwards, where she later migrated along with most of her family (eventually dying in Brazil). Arrowsmith surmises one of the figures here resembles the great Shantiniketan trained modernist Angelo da Fonseca (1902-1967), whom Trindade loved and respected, and had sought to marry, but was not permitted to do so by her parents for various issues including caste. That particular mystery may never be solved, but this fantastic painting is an urgent reminder that even the basic facts about this hugely significant artist have been obscured or forgotten due to sheer neglect. I was shocked to see her described in Wikipedia as an “American artist” which perhaps is not so surprising after all because her father is even more absurdly referred to as “Portuguese painter.” There are several other modern and contemporary Indian artistic families, but perhaps none as historically significant as Trindade père et fille. António Xavier Trindade was born in Sanguem in 1870, and went from being a star student at Sir Jamshetjee Jeejeebhoy School of Art in Bombay to the first Indian to be appointed Superintendent of the Reay Workshop. He was an esteemed portrait painter, referred to in his own lifetime as “Rembrandt of the East” so already eminent by the time Angela was born in 1909 (if you have not seen it, please hasten to Fundação Oriente in Fontainhas to view his masterpiece 1912 self-portrait). Along with his wife Florentina (there is another superb portrait of her in the FO collection) raised eight talented and unconventional children, whom Angela also devoted her life to supporting, never herself marrying, and remaining childless. There is this poignant correspondence in the Gracias book: “believe me darling, I have no regrets. I dedicated my whole life to my family. Every moment of my life was a life of service and loving care for each one of you. My beloved darlings, my brothers’ and sisters’ children were as precious as ever to me as if they were mine – yet I detached myself from being possessive or hurt, when I was ignored or not understood. This made my relationship with all of you ever closer and forever bound with a love beyond love. No returns or rewards.” In an interesting 2023 essay entitled ‘An Indian artist who helped decolonise Christian art has been relegated to the margins in death’, Kamayani Sharma sums up the Indian art history status quo: “At the first All India Women Artists’ Exhibition in 1936, 27-year-old Ângela Trindade won the gold medal. This was a period when the figure of the professionally trained woman artist was just beginning to emerge in South Asia, with relatively few individuals being able to make a mark that is discernible after nearly a century. Among Trindade’s contemporaries at Bombay’s JJ School of Art was Ambika Dhurandhar, another accomplished artist whose design for a commemorative scroll box for the Maharaja of Baroda’s diamond jubilee won a prize in 1935. Elsewhere, in 1934, the Indo-Hungarian painter Amrita Sher-Gil arrived in Simla with a view to setting up her studio in India. Since the mid-’30s, the three artists’ careers have enjoyed varying fates: Dhurandhar’s work is held largely in private collections and seldom exhibited, while Sher-Gil is one of India’s most famous artists, accorded the status of a navratna by the Indian government in the 1970s, her work permanently on view at the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi. Trindade’s visibility is somewhere in the middle: while low-profile, her paintings are surprisingly accessible – on public display in Panjim’s old Fontainhas neighbourhood. The ground-floor gallery of Fundação Oriente exhibits works by two important Indian artists, the father daughter pair of António Xavier Trindade and Ângela Trindade. While the place of the elder Trindade in the story of modern Indian art is beginning to be acknowledged, Ângela remains on its margins.” I shared the scan from Gomes with Ranjit Hoskote, the invaluable critic, curator and poet, who kindly sent me this assessment: “Angela Trindade’s evocation of ‘The Coronation of Our Lady’ is a visionary embodiment of the cultural renaissance that swept through India between the 1920s and the 1950s, its energy feeding into the anti-colonial struggle liberation but not reducible to it. I emphasize this because the style of painting in evidence here did not simply attempt to revive the Buddhist iconography associated with the Ajanta cave complex, a project cherished as much by Trindade’s teachers at the Sir J J School of Art as by the masters of the Bengal School. Angela Trindade did more – she translated a Christian narrative into a Mahayana Buddhist pictorial language, which allowed her to expand the imaginative horizons of South Asian Christianity (a good two decades before Vatican II set the programme of inculturation in motion). This painting goes beyond a national framework to embrace the grand transcultural circulation of ideas and images that connected Ajanta to Dunhuang and Bamiyan.” Hoskote says, “through the same gesture, Trindade demonstrated the common ground between seemingly distinct religious traditions, mapping their shared conceptions of compassion, loving-kindness, and grace. In retrospect, we see how Angela Trindade may be situated in a centuries-long lineage of adaptation and confluence by which Christianity, one of India’s oldest religions, present in the subcontinent since the 1st century CE, has consistently maintained a dialogue with its immediate cultural, philosophical and ecological surroundings. The expansive, cosmopolitan impulses of this lineage – I think here, also, of the Rev Thomas Stephens’ Krista purana – form a counterpoint to the Euro-provincialism of the colonial encounter, and flourish beyond it.” Share This Article Facebook Whatsapp Whatsapp Copy Link Previous Article Water bodies or garbage bins?
